techniques.title: Abuse Elevation Control Mechanism
techniques.text: Adversaries may circumvent mechanisms designed to control elevated privileges. In Android this is commonly seen as abuse of mutable PendingIntents (CVE-2021-0938 family), exported activities that grant admin actions, and SmsRetriever / accessibility services elevated beyond their declared purpose.

techniques.title: Steal Application Access Token
techniques.text: Adversaries may steal tokens used to authenticate API calls. In mobile this includes SharedPreferences-stored bearer tokens, Keystore keys lacking biometric binding, FCM device tokens, and OAuth refresh tokens persisted across logout.

techniques.title: Credentials from Password Store
techniques.text: Adversaries may access credential storage in databases, keystores, or password managers. Mobile-specific surfaces include AccountManager.getAuthToken(), AndroidKeyStore entries lacking setUserAuthenticationRequired(true), and webview password-autofill caches.

techniques.title: Adversary-in-the-Middle
techniques.text: Adversaries may position themselves between two communicating endpoints to intercept and modify traffic. Cleartext HTTP traffic, missing cert pinning, and custom TrustManager / HostnameVerifier implementations are the typical mobile entry points.

techniques.title: Access Notifications
techniques.text: Adversaries may collect data from notifications. Apps registering NotificationListenerService have full read access to every notification on the device, including 2FA codes and bank-app push alerts.

techniques.title: Exploitation for Privilege Escalation
techniques.text: Adversaries may exploit software vulnerabilities to gain elevated privileges. Memory-corruption bugs in JNI native libraries and unsafe deserialization sinks (ObjectInputStream.readObject, polymorphic Gson/Jackson) are the most common mobile-app shapes.

techniques.title: Exploit Enterprise Resources
techniques.text: Adversaries may exploit resources reachable from the mobile network position. Mobile SSRF (D_083) reaching cloud IMDS endpoints (169.254.169.254) or RFC1918 ranges through user-controlled URL inputs is the canonical pattern.

techniques.title: Compromise Application Executable
techniques.text: Adversaries may modify the executable code of an installed application to maintain persistence. Insecure in-app updaters that install APKs without signature checks (D_030) and dynamic code loading from writable paths (D_005) enable this.

techniques.title: Clipboard Data
techniques.text: Adversaries may read the contents of the system clipboard. Apps with foreground access can use ClipboardManager.getPrimaryClip; background readers (D_036) bypass user expectation, particularly on Android <10 where clipboard read was unrestricted.

techniques.title: Command and Scripting Interpreter
techniques.text: Adversaries may abuse command and script interpreters to execute commands. Runtime.exec / ProcessBuilder reached via unsafe reflection chains (D_033) or DexClassLoader on attacker-influenceable paths gives an attacker command execution as the app UID.

techniques.title: Encrypted Channel
techniques.text: Adversaries may use encrypted channels to evade detection. From a defender perspective, weakly-pinned TLS (N_001/N_005) and accept-all TrustManager (N_008) implementations downgrade this protection and let analysts MITM.

techniques.title: Exfiltration Over C2 Channel
techniques.text: Adversaries may steal data by exfiltrating it over an existing command and control channel. PII shipped to third-party analytics or ads hosts (D_013) is the data-leakage twin of this technique inside legitimate mobile apps.
